Current evidence: The physical therapy management of developmental coordination disorder (DCD) is informed
by a clinical practice guideline (CPG) published in 2020 (2020 DCD CPG).1 To support implementation of the 2020
DCD CPG,1 3 resources were developed by the American Physical Therapy Association Academy of Pediatrics (APTA
Pediatrics).2
Gap in the evidence: The 2020 DCD CPG1 does not include evidence published after 2020.
How does this study fill this evidence gap? This 2026 DCD CPG was updated using evidence on the physical
therapy management of DCD through January 2025, the Guideline Development Group’s clinical and professional
experience, trends in practice changes, and external review both by the general public and content experts, including a
teenager with DCD and parents/caregivers of children with DCD.
Implications of all the evidence: This 2026 DCD CPG informs the physical therapy management of DCD on: physi­
cal therapy contributions to the diagnostic process, examination and evaluation including recommended outcome meas­
ures, collaborative plans of care including referral to other providers and dosage considerations, shared ­decision-making
to establish meaningful goals and home programs, evidence-based interventions including task-oriented approaches
to intervention and community physical activities, progress monitoring, transition to annual or semi-annual reassess­
ments, implementation and compliance recommendations, and research recommendations.
Background: Developmental coordination disorder
(DCD) affects 5% of school-age children and is charac­
terized by impaired motor coordination and planning,
not better explained by other conditions. Motor diffi­
culties negatively impact school performance, activi­
ties of daily living, and participation with family and
peers and may persist into adulthood. The 2020 DCD
Clinical Practice Guideline (2020 DCD CPG) set stand­
ards for the physical therapy management of children
with DCD. Purpose: This 2026 DCD CPG provides
an updated reference for physical therapists, families,
healthcare professionals, educators, and research­
ers to improve clinical outcomes and inform future
research. Results and Conclusions: The 2026 DCD
CPG addresses: physical therapy contributions to the
diagnostic process, examination/evaluation including
recommended outcome measures; collaborative plans
of care including referral to other providers and dosage
considerations; shared decision-making to establish
meaningful goals and home programs; evidence-based
interventions including task-oriented approaches and
community physical activities; progress monitoring;
implementation and compliance recommendations;
and research recommendations. (Pediatr Phys Ther
2026;38:297–333)
Key words: clinical practice guidelines, developmental
coordination disorder, pediatrics, physical therapy

chunks.text:
298 Sargent et al
The 2026 Developmental Coordination Disorder Clinical
Practice Guideline (2026 DCD CPG) is an update of the 2020
Developmental Coordination Disorder Clinical Practice Guide­
line (2020 DCD CPG).1 It is intended as a reference document
to guide physical therapists’ (PT) practice; to recommend
research on the physical therapy management of ­developmental
coordination disorder (DCD); and to inform other ­healthcare
professionals, families, and educators about physical therapy
­evidence–based practice for DCD.
Critical appraisal methods, assigning levels of evidence to
the literature, and summarizing evidence to assign grades to the
recommended action statements followed international meth­
odologies of evidence-based practice.3 This document provides
the levels of evidence and grades (Tables 1 and 2) used to derive
the 11 action statements (Table 3) that are organized into 3
major headings: (1) physical therapy examination, evaluation,
and referral of children with coordination difficulties, at risk for
DCD or diagnosed with DCD; (2) physical therapy intervention
for children at risk for DCD or diagnosed with DCD; and (3)
monitoring children at risk for DCD or diagnosed with DCD.
The clinical practice guideline (CPG) action statements and
supporting evidence are organized using the National Academy
of Medicine criteria for trustworthy CPGs.4 Evidence tables on
examination, task-oriented approaches to intervention, and
evidence-informed community physical activities are available
in Supplemental Digital Content 1, Tables S2–S5, available at:
follow each action statement.

chunks.text:
[A] Action Statement 1: DOCUMENT TO INFORM THE 4 DSM-5-TR CRITERIA. Physical therapists who are
examining a child referred for coordination difficulties should document the following to inform the 4 DSM-5-TR
criteria when the signs and symptoms are suggestive of DCD. The following are recommended to inform each
criterion when referring for a formal diagnosis:
• Criterion A (motor performance deficits): MABC-3;
• Criterion B (participation and ADL limitations): Little DCDQ or DCDQ;
• Criterion C (early onset): parent/caregiver’s report of onset of coordination concerns; and
• Criterion D (no exclusionary conditions): parent/caregiver’s report of other medical conditions and the physical
therapist’s evaluation suggest that the motor performance deficits are not better explained by another condition
affecting movement.
(Evidence Quality: I; Recommendation Strength: Strong)
New
[P] Action Statement 2: COMPLETE A HISTORY AND SYSTEMS REVIEW. Physical therapists should obtain and
document a comprehensive history and systems review for a child referred for coordination difficulties, at risk for
DCD, or diagnosed with DCD. (Evidence Quality: V; Recommendation Strength: Best Practice)
Revised, Updated
[A] Action Statement 3: EXAMINE ACTIVITY LIMITATIONS AND PHYSICAL PERFORMANCE. When a child
presents with coordination difficulties, physical therapists should perform a comprehensive physical therapy exam­
ination and evaluation targeting participation priorities, which should include any combination of:
• Measures of participation;
• Measures of activity;
• Movement analysis/observation;
• Ecological assessment, if warranted; and
• Assessments of body functions and structures, if warranted.
(Evidence Quality: I; Recommendation Strength: Strong)
Revised, Upgraded
[B] Action Statement 4: USE SHARED DECISION-MAKING TO ESTABLISH MEANINGFUL GOALS. For chil­
dren at risk for DCD or diagnosed with DCD, physical therapists should use shared decision-making with the child
and family to establish measurable child-centered functional goals based on their participation priorities during the
initial and subsequent examinations. (Evidence Quality: II; Recommendation Strength: Moderate)
New
[P] Action Statement 5: ESTABLISH COLLABORATIVE PLAN OF CARE. Physical therapists should use shared
decision-making with the child, family, and other relevant service providers to establish a collaborative plan of
care that may include referral of children to their primary care provider when signs and symptoms are suggestive
of DCD and the child has not been diagnosed, and if there are red flags or concerns for other medical conditions.
(Evidence Quality: V; Recommendation Strength: Best Practice)
New
II. PHYSICAL THERAPY INTERVENTION FOR CHILDREN AT RISK FOR DCD OR DIAGNOSED WITH DCDa
[A] Action Statement 6: USE TASK-ORIENTED APPROACHES TO INTERVENTION.

chunks.text:
For children at risk for
DCD or diagnosed with DCD, physical therapists should use and document task-oriented approaches to inter­
vention, guided by the child’s goals and meaningful activities, with body functions and structures interventions
used only when directly supporting the achievement of the child’s goals. (Evidence Quality: I; Recommendation
Strength: Strong)
Revised, Updated
[A] Action Statement 7: RECOMMEND COMMUNITY PHYSICAL ACTIVITIES. After appraising the appro­
priateness for the child, physical therapists should recommend evidence-informed, community physical activities
to complement task-oriented approaches to intervention for children at risk for DCD or diagnosed with DCD.
(Evidence Quality: I; Recommendation Strength: Strong)
Revised, Updated
[A] Action Statement 8: USE SMALL GROUP OR INDIVIDUAL SESSIONS. For children at risk for DCD or
diagnosed with DCD, physical therapists should document and deliver interventions using individual (1:1) or
small group (1:4–6) sessions. (Evidence Quality: I; Recommendation Strength: Strong)
Updated
[B] Action Statement 9: PROVIDE APPROPRIATE INTERVENTION DOSAGE. For children at risk for DCD or
diagnosed with DCD, physical therapists should design episodic intervention plans with high practice frequencies,
using a combination of direct services and home, school, and community opportunities. (Evidence Quality: II;
Recommendation Strength: Moderate)
Revised
[B] Action Statement 10: USE SHARED DECISION-MAKING TO ESTABLISH A HOME PROGRAM. For
children at risk for DCD or diagnosed with DCD, physical therapists should use shared decision-making with the
child, parents/caregivers, and other relevant service providers to establish a meaningful home program that may
include education, coaching, motor skill practice, or community physical activities to support attainment of the
child’s goals and participation in activities with family and peers. (Evidence Quality: II; Recommendation Strength:
Moderate)
Revised, Updated

Background of the 2026 Developmental Coordination
Disorder (DCD) Clinical Practice Guideline
DCD is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by
impaired motor acquisition and function that persistently
interferes with activities of daily living (ADLs), academic pro­
ductivity, vocational activities, leisure, and play.6 Although the
provision of physical therapy examination and intervention
for coordination difficulties is well documented, individuals
with coordination difficulties are often referred with diagno­
ses of dyspraxia, sensory integration disorder, or hypermobility
rather than DCD.7 The 2019 update of the European Academy
of Childhood Disability (EACD) International Clinical Practice
Recommendations provided general healthcare recommenda­
tions for the assessment and management of DCD.8 The 2020
DCD CPG was developed to delineate specific physical therapy
recommendations.1 The 2026 DCD CPG updates the evidence
on the management of children with coordination difficulties, at
risk for DCD, or diagnosed with DCD, specific to physical ther­
apy services. Current conventions are to update CPGs every 5
years. To support implementation of the DCD CPGs, resources
developed by the Academy of Pediatric Physical Therapy of the
American Physical Therapy Association (APTA Pediatrics) for
PTs, other medical professionals, and parents/caregivers of chil­
dren at risk for DCD or diagnosed with DCD are available at
Purposes of the 2026 Developmental Coordination Disorder

The 2026 DCD CPG update intends to assist PTs with exam­
ination, evaluation, and intervention of children with coordi­
nation difficulties, at risk for DCD, or diagnosed with DCD, to
optimize activity and participation outcomes. It also informs
the need for continued research related to the physical therapy
management of DCD. This document replaces the 2020 DCD
CPG.1
The purposes of the 2026 DCD CPG are to:
• Appraise the current best evidence and recommend
physical therapy examination and interventions for chil­
dren (ages 3–18 years) with coordination difficulties, at
risk for DCD, or diagnosed with DCD, to provide guid­
ance and reduce variation in care.
• Inform healthcare professionals, families, and educators
about physical therapy best practices for DCD.
• Identify areas for research to improve the evidence for
physical therapy management of DCD.

tematic reviews (SR) on physical therapy examination and
evaluation9 and physical therapy interventions10 that summa­
rize literature from January 2018 to June 2024, and critical
appraisals of literature published from June 2024 to January

chunks.text:
therapy management of children at risk for DCD from ages 3
to 5 years, the age range of this guideline has been expanded to
3 to 18 years of age. It is assumed that PTs using this guideline
have experience working with pediatric populations.
The CPG addresses the following:
• PTs’ roles related to the diagnosis of DCD using the
Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders,
Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR)6 criteria and the
patient management process.
• Recommendations for screening, referral, examination,
evaluation, intervention, and reassessment in settings
where physical therapy services may be provided, within
the International Classification of Functioning, Disability
and Health categories of body functions and structures
(BFS), activity, and participation.
This CPG does not specifically address:
• Handwriting examination and intervention, which is not
a common area of expertise for PTs.
• Executive function or other psychological constructs
that are better addressed by psychology.
• Management of children with DCD and coexisting neu­
rodevelopmental or neurodivergent conditions. For chil­
dren with DCD and coexisting conditions such as autism
spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity
disorder (ADHD), or sensory differences, the PT will
need to complete a thorough examination that addresses
all areas of concern and coexisting conditions, then con­
sider integration of evidence-based interventions for
these coexisting conditions with those for DCD.

Statement of Intent
This CPG is intended to inform pediatric PTs, family members,
educators, and other healthcare providers (eg, primary care pro­
viders, occupational therapists, and psychologists) who work
with children aged 3 to 18 years with coordination difficulties, at
risk for DCD, or diagnosed with DCD. This CPG does not estab­
lish a legal standard of care. Rather, it provides a synthesis of cur­
rent, evidence-based physical therapy. This CPG is a summary of
physical therapy recommendations, developed and reviewed in
collaboration with healthcare practitioners, educators, parents of
children with DCD, and teenagers with DCD.
The action statements included in this guideline are intended
to serve as recommendations, not mandates. Following these
recommendations does not ensure a specific outcome for every
child, nor do they encompass all methods or approaches for
achieving similar outcomes. Clinical decision-making should
be individualized and involve collaboration with the child and
their family, taking into account their values, expectations, and
preferences; relevant clinical information; available examination
and intervention options; and the clinician’s professional scope
and expertise. However, it is recommended that significant
departures from accepted guidelines should be documented in
medical or educational records, including a rationale for such
decisions; clinicians are strongly encouraged to publish the clin­
ical reasoning and results of alternative approaches.

The Guideline Development Group (GDG) was approved by
APTA Pediatrics to update the 2020 DCD CPG1 in accordance
with Academy procedures. APTA Pediatrics did not influence
the guideline content, and there was no external funding to
support this CPG revision. The purpose, scope, and content
build on the 2020 DCD CPG.
Search Strategy
This 2026 DCD CPG update is based on 2 SRs of the physical
therapy evidence for examination, evaluation, prognosis, and
intervention of DCD from January 2018 to July 2024. Refer to
Long et al9 and Iwamoto et al10 for details of the protocol registra­
tion, search strategy, study selection, study appraisal, data extrac­
tion, and results for the 49 included studies; 33 studies informed
physical therapy examination and evaluation, and 16 studies
informed physical therapy intervention of children with DCD.
The 2026 DCD CPG used the SR search protocol
from Iwamoto et al10 and Long et al9 to include evidence
post July 2024; refer to PROSPERO, registration number
CRD42024510963.11 A comprehensive search was conducted
from July 2024 to January 2025 by a research librarian of
8 databases (CINAHL, clinicaltrials.gov, Cochrane library,
Embase, PEDro, PsycINFO, PubMed, and Web of Science).
Search terms included pediatric, DCD, and concepts related
to physical therapy assessment, intervention, and prognosis
for DCD. Searches were not restricted by language. The full
search strategy by database is in Supplemental Digital Con­
References of included studies were reviewed and experts in
the field were contacted to identify additional relevant studies.

Studies were included based on the following criteria:

teenagers with DCD, parents/caregivers or teachers of chil­
dren with DCD, and PTs that manage children with DCD that
directly inform the physical therapy management of DCD.
Studies were excluded based on the following criteria: (1)
studies previously included in the 2020 DCD CPG,1 (2) con­
ference abstracts and dissertations, (3) literature and scoping
reviews, (4) studies published in a language other than English
when an adequate English translation could not be obtained
through translation software, and (5) qualitative studies that
identified a greater need for access to physical therapy but did
not inform the content of physical therapy management of DCD.
Study Selection
Study titles and abstracts were screened using Covidence SR soft­
ware (Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia; available
ria, followed by full-text review. During the screening and fulltext review, pairs of 10 reviewers independently reviewed the
studies, data were compared for agreement, and discrepancies
were resolved through discussion. Four studies were excluded
during the full-text review: 2 for ineligible outcome,12,13 1 for
ineligible study design,14 and 1 for ineligible statistical analysis.15
Study Appraisal
Pairs of 10 reviewers independently appraised the studies
using a risk of bias tool appropriate for the study type, data
were compared for agreement, and discrepancies were resolved
through discussion. Risk of bias was assessed using the Risk
of Bias in Systematic Reviews (ROBIS)16 for SRs of assessment
tools, Consensus-Based Standards for the Selection of Health
Measurement Instruments (COSMIN)17 for studies on the
psychometric properties of assessment tools, A Measurement
Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews 2 (AMSTAR-2)18 for SRs of
interventions, the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB2)19
for RCTs, the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) for
and the Quality In Prognosis Studies (QUIPS)20 for prognostic
studies. Sources of funding were assessed to determine con­
flicts of interest.
Data Extraction
Data were extracted to maintain consistency with the 2020
DCD CPG1 and the two 2025 DCD SRs.9,10 Refer to Supple­
links.lww.com/PPT/A690. Data elements extracted from each
study were determined by mutual consensus of the GDG, then
extracted independently by pairs of 10 reviewers; data were
compared for agreement and discrepancies were resolved
through discussion.

links.lww.com/PPT/A690, which combines the searches from
the 2 SRs9,10 and the additional search to update the evidence.
Eight additional studies were included: 2 SRs21,22 informed
physical therapy examination and evaluation, and 3 SRs,23–25 2
RCTs,26,27 and 1 qualitative study28 informed intervention.
Refer to Supplemental Digital Content 1, Table S2, available
quality rating, overall quality rating, aim, tests and measures
reviewed, date range and studies, quality of evidence, and clin­
ical implications of the SRs of tests and measures, including the
2 new SRs.21,22 Refer to Supplemental Digital Content 1, Table
on the AMSTAR-2 score, overall quality rating, aim, interven­
tion of interest and outcome measures, date range and studies,
quality of evidence, relative effects, and clinical implications
of the SRs interventions, including the 3 new SRs.23–25 Refer to
Supplemental Digital Content 1, Tables S4 and S5, available
design, level of evidence, RoB2 score, participants’ diagnos­
tic criteria, intervention groups and participants, intervention
parameters and setting, interventions, outcome measures, and
clinical implications of the RCTs, including the 2 new RCTs.15,27
Please note, these tables include SRs and RCTs from the 2020
DCD CPG,29–36 the 2 SRs that informed this guideline,23,37,38 and
the new SRs and RCTs included in this 2026 DCD CPG to pro­
vide a summary of the strongest evidence. Other study types
were not included in the tables.
One new study was not included in the evidence tables
because it was not an SR or an RCT, so the results are described
here. Schoenmaker et al28 sought to describe the teaching strate­
gies used by PTs in individual physical therapy sessions of chil­
dren with DCD; the study had adequate methodological quality.
By analyzing 18 videos of physical therapy sessions using the
OPTIMAL Strategies Observational Tool, they found that PTs
generally used strategies to support autonomy (compared with
therapist-controlled strategies) and enhance expectations (in
contrast to lowering expectations) and used internal and external
focus of attention to a similar extent. In addition, they found that
strategies were used in combination almost half of the time.28

rency and consistency with the updated research literature by the

was informed by the evidence, the GDG’s clinical and profes­
sional experience, and trends in practice changes. Changes were
proposed by GDG members and discussed by the group until
consensus was achieved, then edits were made to the CPG.
External Review Procedures
A first draft of the 2026 DCD CPG was reviewed by an advi­
sory panel representing teenagers with DCD, parents of chil­
dren with DCD, and representatives from academia, education,
medicine, occupational therapy, and physical therapy practice
and research. A rating scale to assess clarity and implementa­
tion feasibility and an open-ended request for comments and
edits were used to gather feedback. The first-round suggested
edits were discussed by the GDG until consensus was achieved
and changes were made to the CPG. Then, the document was
reviewed by a member of the APTA Pediatrics and posted for
public review on the APTA Pediatrics website. Invitations to
review were distributed to APTA Pediatrics members via its
electronic newsletters and through a social media posting.
Nonmembers could review if notified by APTA Pediatrics mem­
bers. The same rating scale to assess clarity and implementation
feasibility and an open-ended request for comments and edits
were used to gather feedback. The public review comments
and suggested edits were discussed by the GDG until consen­
sus was achieved and changes were made to the CPG.
All 11 action statements rated by the advisory panel and
public were rated as clear and feasible by over 70% of review­
ers, except for Action Statement 9 on providing appropriate
intervention dosage that only 65% of reviewers rated as feasible
and 35% as somewhat feasible. Suggested edits were addressed
to clarify content and add additional items under risk, harm,
and cost. Some reviewers requested production of parent, PT,
and healthcare provider support documents, which were for­
warded to the 2026 DCD CPG knowledge translation team.
Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation II
(AGREE II) Review
This CPG was evaluated by 4 external reviewers using Appraisal
of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation II (AGREE II).39
Domain scores for the 2026 DCD CPG ranged from 88% to
98%. The 4 reviewers agreed to recommend the 2026 DCD
CPG for use. AGREE II scores were discussed by the GDG and
edits were made to the CPG to address lower-scoring items by
clarifying methodology. The final 2026 DCD CPG draft was
submitted to Pediatric Physical Therapy for editorial review.

Details on the development of the guideline are in Supplemen­
A690.
Plan for Updating the Guideline
Per current standards, this CPG will be reviewed for potential
updates or reaffirmation within 5 years as the body of evidence
expands. The guideline revision will be organized by Megan
Frazier, PT, DPT, PCS.
Language
The 2020 DCD CPG has been referenced up to this point, but
will be used without reference hereafter. In contrast, this docu­
ment is referred to as the “2026 DCD CPG” and the DSM-5-TR
diagnosis of DCD will be referred to as “DCD”. The phrase
“primary care provider” is inclusive of pediatricians, develop­
mental pediatricians, family or specialist physicians, advanced
practice nurses, physician assistants, or other primary health­
care providers. In this guideline, educators, coaches, or other
community activity providers are referred to as “other relevant
service providers” because they may play an important role in
the life of the child and their family.
This CPG discusses the physical therapy management of
children with either coordination difficulties, at risk for DCD, or
diagnosed with DCD. Children referred to physical therapy due
to concerns about coordination before having a formal diag­
nosis are described in this CPG as a “child with coordination
difficulties.” A child may be described as “at risk for DCD” or
“probable DCD” during the examination process when some of
the DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria for DCD are identified. A child
“diagnosed with DCD” has met all 4 of the DSM-5-TR criteria
and has a formal diagnosis of DCD. The term “other or unspec­
ified lack of coordination” may be a familiar International Sta­
tistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems,
version 10 (ICD-10) billing code that is not used as a diagnosis
in this document but is described in Supplemental Digital Con­

chunks.text:
Children with DCD or at risk for DCD often have difficulty
with coordination or motor planning tasks and activities that
their peers typically master. These challenges can affect learn­
ing and social participation during the school years and later
in life. What appears as poor coordination can be caused by
many factors. It is through a comprehensive assessment pro­
cess, ideally with a coordinated team of medical and healthcare
providers, that DCD can be differentially identified, even when
combined with other conditions.
DCD is an underrecognized and undersupported condition
within the United States.7 Literature is evolving to provide a
better understanding of DCD and to support optimal man­
agement and care for children with coordination difficulties,
at risk for DCD, and diagnosed with DCD. This section pro­
vides a synopsis of the most recent literature, including inform­
ing the diagnostic process using the DCD DSM-5-TR, DCD

chunks.text:
308 Sargent et al
neurophysiology, psychological and social consequences, DCD
throughout the lifespan, and physical therapy management. Informing the Diagnostic Process for Developmental
Coordination Disorder
DCD is defined as a neurodevelopmental disorder and subcate­
gorized as a motor disorder in the DSM-5-TR.6 According to the
DSM-5-TR, all 4 diagnostic components (Criteria A through D)
must be met to confirm a diagnosis of DCD. Table 4 lists the
required DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria. There is consensus that diagnosis and management of DCD
requires an interprofessional team approach.40,41 This team may
include the child and caregivers, the primary care provider, pedi­
atric psychiatrists and neurologists, PTs, occupational therapists,
speech-language pathologists, and other relevant service provid­
ers. Service coordination and collaboration are crucial to address
function, participation, and the prevention of secondary conse­
quences, while maintaining a child-centered and family-informed
approach. Children diagnosed with DCD should also be screened
for co-occurring conditions, such as ADHD and ASD.42 Pediatric
PTs contribute their expertise in child development, motor con­
trol, motor learning, movement observation, functional training,
and clinical reasoning. They often serve as key advocates and
coordinators in both clinical and educational settings. While PTs in the United States are not licensed to inde­
pendently diagnose DCD, data gathered during a comprehen­
sive physical therapy examination can contribute meaningfully
to the diagnostic process. This data may support other findings
used by a multidisciplinary team, inclusive of a PT, to arrive at
a diagnosis.1,6,8,43 A formal diagnosis of DCD is typically made
when a child is 5 years of age or older, as the diagnostic criteria
can be more accurately applied then; however, signs of motor
coordination difficulties may be evident much earlier. Neurophysiology of Developmental Coordination Disorder
Research advances challenge the notion that DCD is mere
clumsiness, highlighting instead a complex neurodevelopmen­
tal condition involving atypical sensory integration44,45 and
increased cognitive demands during motor tasks.46,47 Motor
control difficulties common in DCD include difficulty with
executive function, learning of new internal models, and dif­
ficulty with predictive control,48–50 all of which are linked to
cognition.

chunks.text:
Neurophysiology studies provide growing evidence
that children with DCD have altered development, activation,
and function of cortical networks compared with typically
developing peers,49–53 children with ASD,54 or children with
developmental dyslexia.55 The prefrontal cortex shows greater
activation in children with DCD during complex motor tasks,
reflecting decreased automaticity.46,47 Meanwhile, brain regions
associated with timing, motor control, and motor learning,
such as the primary sensorimotor cortex, posterior superior
temporal gyrus, cerebellum, and supplementary motor area,
show lower activation in children with DCD compared with
typically developing peers.48,56,57 Children with DCD show
greater cortical activity on functional near-infrared spectros­
copy when performing dual tasks,46,58 further suggesting that
DCD is a motor–cognitive disability.46
In addition to the cognitive differences, neurophysiology
studies also accentuate the importance of sensorimotor inte­
gration differences in DCD. Children with DCD integrate visual
and motor information differently than their peers53 and use
altered patterns of selection and prioritization between visual
and somatosensory inputs.48,53,57 These sensorimotor differ­
ences negatively affect predictive motor control48,53,57 and
increase cognitive interference.46,58 These outcomes underscore
a broader understanding that DCD is not simply a motor dis­
order, but one that fundamentally alters sensory, motor, and
cognitive processing.48
Psychosocial Consequences Associated With
Developmental Coordination Disorder
Children with DCD experience difficulties in self-concept related to
their decreased levels of physical competence.48,59,60 Physical condi­
tions frequently associated with DCD include hypotonicity or joint
laxity,61 balance deficits,49 being overweight or obese,61 and lower
levels of physical activity.62 Children at risk for DCD demonstrate

Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR): Diagnostic Criteria Description for Developmental
Coordination Disorder and Criteria Key6
Diagnostic Criteria Description
Criteria Key
A
The acquisition and execution of coordinated motor skills are substantially below that expected, given the individual’s chron­
ological age and opportunity for skill learning and use. Difficulties are manifested as clumsiness (eg, dropping or bumping
into objects) as well as slowness and inaccuracy of performance of motor skills (eg, catching an object, using scissors or
cutlery, handwriting, riding a bike, or participating in sports).
Motor perfor­
mance deficits
B
The motor skills deficit in criterion A significantly and persistently interferes with activities of daily living appropriate to
chronological age (eg, self-care and self-maintenance) and affects academic/school productivity, prevocational and voca­

slower running speeds and lower cardiorespiratory fitness, both of
which continue to worsen as they age compared with their peers.63
Body composition and limitations in muscle strength and endur­
ance, anaerobic capacity, and physical activity are all associated
with poor motor performance in children with DCD.63,64
Children with DCD may also experience a range of psycho­
social challenges that contribute to a decreased quality of life,49,65
including elevated rates of depression and anxiety.59,61,66 Social
difficulties are common with reduced peer interactions, increased
risk of bullying,60,67–69 and less engagement in school and commu­
nity activities.70 Given these long-term consequences, early inter­
vention is important for maximizing opportunities for success. Developmental Coordination Disorder Throughout the
Lifespan
The literature is expanding to include younger and older indi­
viduals at risk for or diagnosed with DCD. Early indicators of
DCD can include delays in achieving motor milestones,12,13 fre­
quent tripping (clumsy gait),71 less participation during recess,63
decreased endurance with physical activity,72 and struggles with
fine motor tasks such as handwriting and preparing a meal.73
Although these signs may not meet full diagnostic criteria, they
can suggest an increased risk for DCD. In such cases, stand­
ardized assessments and parent/caregiver or teacher completed
questionnaires can aid in the early identification of motor coor­
dination difficulties,74 even if a formal diagnosis is deferred until
age 5.9,75 Early identification and management of DCD may
improve long-term prognosis for children with DCD.25
Children with DCD continue to have symptoms into ado­
lescence and adulthood.68,76–78 Adolescents with DCD may
struggle with academic performance due to problems with
organization, written expression, practical tasks, and participa­
tion in physical education.74,79 They often report higher levels
of anxiety and lower levels of resilience, self-efficacy, and qual­
ity of life when compared with typical peers.

chunks.text:
These challenges
can further influence long-term outcomes, including reduced
participation in higher education and limitations in employ­
ment opportunities, particularly in jobs requiring manual dex­
terity or motor coordination.80 Participants in a recent study
described the far-reaching implications of living with DCD,
noting struggles across all areas of life: at home, in school, with
friends, and within their communities.78 Despite these chal­
lenges, they also reported having access to various resources
and strategies that helped them cope with daily difficulties.76,78
Physical Therapy Management of Developmental
Coordination Disorder
Effective management of DCD requires a comprehensive
physical therapy examination and evaluation that reflects the
heterogeneity of this population.9 An assessment of activity
and participation limitations, related BFS impairments, and
environmental and contextual barriers should be included.81
Task-oriented approaches are recommended to enhance motor
skills, with a focus on improving participation in personally
meaningful activities and goals.10 In addition to task-oriented
approaches, interventions may also target relevant underly­
ing BFS impairments that directly impact function, as well as
strategies to mitigate environmental and contextual barriers
that hinder participation.49 Figure 1 and Figure S1 describe the
processes included in physical therapy management of DCD;
clinicians may find it useful for educating children with DCD,
­families, primary care providers, teachers, and other relevant ser­
vice providers.

chunks.text:
[A] Action Statement 1: DOCUMENT TO INFORM THE 4
DSM-5-TR CRITERIA. PTs who are examining a child referred
for coordination difficulties should document the following to
inform the 4 DSM-5-TR criteria when the signs and symptoms
are suggestive of DCD. The following are recommended to
inform each criterion when referring for a formal diagnosis:
• Criterion A (motor performance deficits): MABC-3;
• Criterion B (participation and ADL limitations): Little
DCDQ or DCDQ;
• Criterion C (early onset): parent/caregiver’s report of
onset of coordination concerns; and
• Criterion D (no exclusionary conditions): parent/car­
egiver’s report of other medical conditions and/or the
PT’s evaluation suggests that the motor performance dif­
ficulties are not better explained by another condition
affecting movement.
(Evidence Quality: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong)
Action Statement Profile. Aggregate Evidence Quality:
Level I, based on CPGs, SRs, and studies on the psychometric
properties of the MABC-3, Little DCDQ, and DCDQ.
Benefits:
• These 4 foci of information inform the DSM-5-TR crite­
ria for a formal diagnosis of DCD.
• These 4 criteria may help parent(s)/caregiver(s) better
appreciate the complex nature of their child’s coordina­
tion challenges.
• Conducting standardized tests may elicit signs of other
conditions needing follow-up.
• Standardized, norm-referenced motor tests can deter­
mine the degree of motor performance difficulty relevant
to the DSM-5-TR criteria.

Extensive evidence underscores
the MABC-284 as the most commonly used and studied test in
DCD with robust normative data and moderate- to high-­quality
evidence supporting its measurement properties.22 Addition­
ally, recent research has demonstrated that the MABC-2, when
administered at age 3 years to those born very preterm, has
excellent sensitivity and moderate specificity in predicting a
DCD diagnosis at 4.5 years.85
Other standardized clinical tests with adequate measure­
ment properties to inform DSM-5-TR Criterion A (motor perfor­
mance deficits) in decreasing order of the quality and availability
of evidence include the DCDDaily,86 Performance and Fitness
test battery (PERF-FIT),87 Korperkoordinationstest Fur Kinder
(KTK),88 Bruininks–Oseretsky Test of Motor Proficiency, 3rd edi­
tion (BOT-3),89 and Test of Gross Motor Development, 3rd edi­
tion (TGMD-3).90 For a summary of each standardized clinical
test and its measurement properties, refer to Huang et al.22
DSM-5-TR Criterion B (Participation and ADL Limi­
tations): DSM-5-TR Criterion B (participation and ADL lim­
itations) states that a child’s “motor skills deficit” described in
­Criterion A significantly and persistently interferes with “activ­
ities of daily living appropriate to chronological age (eg, selfcare and self-maintenance) and impacts upon academic/school
productivity, prevocational and vocational activities, leisure,
and play.”6
For children aged 3 to 4 years, the Little DCDQ is rec­
ommended to contribute evidence relevant to DSM-5-TR
Criterion B (participation and ADL limitations). The Little
DCDQ is clinically feasible since it is a 15-item parent ques­
ca/. There is moderate- to high-quality evidence supporting
its reliability and validity as a clinical screening tool for chil­
dren at risk for DCD, and cross-cultural adaptations have
been developed with reference norms and cutoff scores.9,22
For children aged 5 to 15 years, the DCDQ91 is recom­
mended to contribute evidence relevant to DSM-5-TR Cri­
terion B (participation and ADL limitations) for 4 reasons. First, the DCDQ is clinically feasible since it is a 15-item
parent questionnaire that can be obtained free of charge at
racy (Summary Receiver Operating Characteristic Area
Under the Curve = 0.90, Standard Error = 0.04) and good
predictive validity (sensitivity = 0.87, specificity = 0.83) with
the DSM-4 and 5. Third, there is moderate- to high-quality
evidence supporting its reliability and validity as a clinical
screening tool for children at risk for DCD.22,92 Last, many

Additional insights into activity limitations related to par­

views, and other questionnaires or checklists, which provide
valuable context to standardized measures. It is important to
note that insufficient reliability has been reported on DCD
questionnaires between parents/caregivers and teachers, so it
may be appropriate to have parents/caregivers, teachers, and
other relevant service providers answer separate DCD ques­
tionnaires for a comprehensive view of the child’s activity lim­
itations across home, school, and community environments.9

development. The PT can use the parent/caregiver’s report of

this criterion. DSM-5-TR Criterion D (No Exclusionary Condi­
tions): DSM-5-TR Criterion D (no exclusionary conditions)
states that the motor performance deficits are not better
explained by an intellectual disability, visual impairment, or
other neurological condition affecting movement (eg, cer­
ebral palsy and muscular dystrophy). The PT can use the
parent/caregiver’s report of other medical conditions and
their clinical judgement if their evaluation suggests that
the motor performance deficits are not better explained by
another condition affecting movement. Research Recommendation:
• Assess the psychometric properties of standardized
assessments used to inform DSM-5-TR Criterion A
(motor performance deficits) and Criterion B (participa­
tion and ADL limitations).
• Clarify the precision of DCD screening procedures to
establish more specific symptoms associated with DSM5-TR Criterion C (early onset) and Criterion D (no exclu­
sionary conditions).

tions): DSM-5-TR Criterion D (no exclusionary conditions)
states that the motor performance deficits are not better
explained by an intellectual disability, visual impairment, or
other neurological condition affecting movement (eg, cer­
ebral palsy and muscular dystrophy). The PT can use the
parent/caregiver’s report of other medical conditions and
their clinical judgement if their evaluation suggests that
the motor performance deficits are not better explained by
another condition affecting movement. Research Recommendation:
• Assess the psychometric properties of standardized
assessments used to inform DSM-5-TR Criterion A
(motor performance deficits) and Criterion B (participa­
tion and ADL limitations).
• Clarify the precision of DCD screening procedures to
establish more specific symptoms associated with DSM5-TR Criterion C (early onset) and Criterion D (no exclu­

SYSTEMS REVIEW. PTs should obtain and document a com­
prehensive history and systems review for a child referred for
coordination difficulties, at risk for DCD, or diagnosed with
DCD. (Evidence Quality: V, Recommendation Strength:
Best Practice)
Action Statement Profile. Aggregate Evidence Quality:
Level V, based on the APTA Guide to PT Practice, review arti­
cles, and expert clinical consensus.

[A] Action Statement 3: EXAMINE ACTIVITY LIMITA­
TIONS AND PHYSICAL PERFORMANCE. When a child
presents with coordination difficulties, PTs should perform a
comprehensive physical therapy examination and evaluation
targeting participation priorities, which should include any
combination of:
• Measures of participation
• Measures of activity
• Movement analysis/observation
• Ecological assessment if warranted
• Assessments of body function and structure (BFS) if war­
ranted
(Evidence Quality: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong)
Action Statement Profile. Aggregate Evidence Quality:
Level I, based on CPGs, SRs, and studies on the psychometric
properties of selected tests. Benefits:
• Documenting participation and activity limitations,
along with BFS impairments that contribute to restricted
participation, is essential for guiding the plan of care. This documentation establishes a baseline for objectively
measuring intervention outcomes and supports appro­
priate referrals to other specialists when indicated.
• Standardized tools or checklists contribute to group data
that may help interpret service impact.
• Movement observations can guide the PT to more spe­
cific tests and measures. Risk, Harm, and Cost:
• Proprietary standardized assessments have associated
costs or online versions may not be compatible with
electronic health record firewalls.
• Standardized motor tests may be misinterpreted if PTs
are unfamiliar with the tests or typical child develop­
ment.
• PTs may require training to enhance consistency and
reliability for using standardized measures.
• Available standardized measures may not address the full
breadth of participation restrictions and activity limita­
tions.
• PTs unfamiliar with DCD may not identify those at risk
for DCD through movement observation/analysis if
unfamiliar with atypical movement profiles. Benefit–Harm Assessment: Preponderance of benefit.

Establishment and Assessment of Participation Priori­
ties: Identifying the child’s participation priorities at the onset
helps guide PTs in performing a child-centered, comprehensive
examination. Participation restrictions are often the primary
reason children with coordination difficulties seek physical
therapy services. Improvements in participation are frequently
considered the ultimate indicators of success for both the child
and their family. A comprehensive assessment of participation
priorities allows the PT to establish relevant, measurable goals
and implement interventions that promote participation. PTs should identify the child’s needs and priorities by per­
forming comprehensive interviews and assessments with the
child, parents/caregivers, and Individualized Educational Plan
(IEP) team if applicable. If children and families/caregivers
experience difficulty expressing their participation priorities,
tools such as the Perceived Efficacy and Goal Setting System
(PEGS),41,107 the Children’s Assessment of Participation and
Enjoyment (CAPE),108 and the Preferences for Activities of
Children (PAC),109 can be used to help identify participation
priorities.

chunks.text:
Standardized Assessment of the Participation Priori­
ties: Standardized participation measures are used to establish
a baseline for the client-centered participation priorities and
are subsequently reassessed following intervention to evaluate
outcomes and effectiveness. The
Canadian
Occupational
Performance
Measure
(COPM)110 is a widely used tool to identify and prioritize the
child’s participation priorities and subsequent goals through
a semi-structured interview. If a child is unable to complete
the COPM (eg, secondary to age), parents/caregivers may
assist and provide answers for the child. This tool promotes
interprofessional practice to meet the child’s needs by facili­
tating ­multidisciplinary intervention goals based on the iden­
tified participation priorities. For children with DCD, recent
low-quality evidence supports that the COPM is responsive
to change with intervention, with a high effect size of 1.65.111
Improvements in participation may be demonstrated through
progress across multiple activity-related goals or by achieving a
singular overarching goal, depending on the participation pri­
orities and the interventions’ foci. To complement standardized measures, additional partic­
ipation data can be obtained through self-reports, parent/car­
egiver interviews, and various questionnaires or checklists.112
These supplementary methods provide valuable insights into
the child’s participation in everyday activities and the potential
impact of interventions. Standardized Assessment of Activity Limitations
Related to Participation Priorities: Many standardized ques­
tionnaires and standardized motor assessments can be used to
assess activity limitations related to participation priorities. For
a comprehensive summary of each standardized assessment
and its measurement properties, refer to Huang et al.22 Addi­
tional insights into activity limitations related to participation
priorities can be obtained through self-reports, caregiver inter­
views, and other questionnaires or checklists, which may pro­
vide individualized context to standardized measures. Standardized Questionnaires: Standardized question­
naires are commonly used to evaluate performance in activ­
ities related to participation. In decreasing order of evidence
strength, they are the DCDQ,91 Little DCDQ,113 DCDDaily-Q,114
MOQ-T,115 and the MABC-3-C.95 Of these questionnaires, the
DCDQ and Little DCDQ have the strongest measurement prop­
erties and quality of evidence for evaluating activity related to
participation in children with DCD,22 and per Action Statement
1, are recommended to inform DSM-5-TR Criterion B (partici­
pation and ADL limitations).

Improvements in participation may be demonstrated through
progress across multiple activity-related goals or by achieving a
singular overarching goal, depending on the participation pri­
orities and the interventions’ foci. To complement standardized measures, additional partic­
ipation data can be obtained through self-reports, parent/car­
egiver interviews, and various questionnaires or checklists.112
These supplementary methods provide valuable insights into
the child’s participation in everyday activities and the potential
impact of interventions. Standardized Assessment of Activity Limitations
Related to Participation Priorities: Many standardized ques­
tionnaires and standardized motor assessments can be used to
assess activity limitations related to participation priorities. For
a comprehensive summary of each standardized assessment
and its measurement properties, refer to Huang et al.22 Addi­
tional insights into activity limitations related to participation
priorities can be obtained through self-reports, caregiver inter­
views, and other questionnaires or checklists, which may pro­
vide individualized context to standardized measures. Standardized Questionnaires: Standardized question­
naires are commonly used to evaluate performance in activ­
ities related to participation. In decreasing order of evidence
strength, they are the DCDQ,91 Little DCDQ,113 DCDDaily-Q,114
MOQ-T,115 and the MABC-3-C.95 Of these questionnaires, the
DCDQ and Little DCDQ have the strongest measurement prop­
erties and quality of evidence for evaluating activity related to
participation in children with DCD,22 and per Action Statement
1, are recommended to inform DSM-5-TR Criterion B (partici­
pation and ADL limitations).

Standardized Motor Assessments: Standardized motor
assessments are commonly used to evaluate motor perfor­
mance related to participation. In decreasing order of ­evidence
strength, they are the MABC-3,83 DCDDaily,86 PERF-FIT,116
KTK,88 BOT-3,89 and TGMD-3.90 Of these motor tests, the
MABC-284 has the strongest measurement properties and qual­
ity of evidence for evaluating motor performance in children
with DCD,22 and per Action Statement 1, the MABC-383 is
recommended to inform DSM-5-TR Criterion A (motor per­
formance deficits). Note that the MABC-3 is recommended by
the GDG due to its updated normative data, but the research
supporting its use in children with DCD was conducted using
the MABC-2. While moderate-quality evidence supports the
use of the MABC-2 as a responsive tool for measuring interven­
tion outcomes for children with DCD,111 the suitability of the
MABC-3 as an outcome measure for physical therapy interven­
tion may vary depending on the child’s participation priorities. Observational Movement Analysis of Participation Pri­
orities: Observational movement analysis describes a child’s
kinesiological strategies for functional task completion.117 A sys­
tematic movement analysis of the activities for which the fam­
ily/caregiver is seeking physical therapy should be documented
and include comments about movement quality ­characteristics. Movement analysis may also occur during standardized tests of
activity and participation. In either instance, movement anal­
ysis may lead to further tests of BFS. For example, if a child is
observed to be lacking control/stability while stair climbing,
the PT may hypothesize deficits in strength or balance and spe­
cifically examine these BFS. A proposed framework for pediatric observational move­
ment analysis includes 11 observable constructs and a
­movement continuum from initial conditions to preparation,
initiation, execution, termination, and outcome.118–120 Prioriti­
zation of movement tasks to be analyzed should be determined
based on the child’s participation goals.

chunks.text:
Observational movement analysis constructs include118–120:
• Symmetry: agreement of external kinetics and kinemat­
ics
• Speed: rate of change of velocity from start to finish
• Amplitude: range of movement
• Alignment: relationship of body segments to one another
• Postural control/verticality
• Stability
• Coordination/smoothness
• Sequencing
• Timing
• Accuracy
• Symptom provocation
Of the observable constructs, children with DCD typically
present with challenges in speed, amplitude, stability,121,122
coordination and smoothness, sequencing, and timing.123 Gait
in this population has been characterized by increased step
width and more variability in double limb stance and stride
time.124 While overall gait speed has been found to be similar to
that of typically developing children, children with DCD use a
strategy of increased cadence with shorter step length to match
pace with their peers.125 The differences observed in gait and
other functional movement are suggestive of less mature pat­
terns than age-matched peers. After completing movement analyses, the PT should deter­
mine whether the activity is not impaired, impaired, or is not
able to be performed or completed, based on the movement
quality characteristics and age norms. This determination
should be followed by consultation with the child’s primary
care provider if there are significant concerns about signs or
symptoms inconsistent with DCD. Ecological Assessment of Participation Priorities if
Warranted: Ecological assessments, also called ­observational
assessments,126,127 are informal checklists used to identify
activity and participation restrictions in the child’s natu­
ral environment. These assessments are frequently used in
school settings due to their alignment with the Individuals
With Disabilities Education Act (IDEA)128 and the Americans
with ­Disabilities Act (ADA).127,129,130 These laws emphasize the
importance of functional performance within the least restric­
tive environment in educational contexts. Ecological assess­
ments allow a PT to identify a child’s strengths, needs, and
barriers to participation. They also enable the PT to observe
the quality of movement and examine possible impairments of
coordination, endurance, strength, and balance that may limit
a child’s participation specific to meaningful environments. By conducting an ecological assessment, PTs can ­pinpoint
the specific parameters that define meaningful participa­
tion for each child, which may not be achievable through an
­impairment-based examination.127
Ecological assessments are well supported as best prac­
tice to assist in developing intervention strategies to directly
improve participation in the child’s natural environment. The
APTA Guide to Physical Therapist Practice43 reinforces this
concept.

chunks.text:
participation priorities and standardized motor assessments
to guide their choice of tests. Aertssen et al133 reviewed 23 studies comparing children
with DCD to their typical developing peers across 28 field-based
tests. These tests were categorized into isometric strength, mus­
cle endurance, muscle power, anaerobic sprint, and test batter­
ies. While the review only recommended the shuttle run item
of the Bruininks–Oseretsky Test of Motor Performance, 2nd
edition (BOT-2) or the 10 × 5-m sprint for assessing anaerobic
capacity in children with DCD, the authors suggested using
the most valid and reliable tools tested in children with typical
development until more evidence becomes available. Key recommendations for assessment tools include133:
• Anaerobic capacity: shuttle run item of the BOT-2,
10 × 5-m sprint
• Isometric strength: handheld dynamometry
• Muscle endurance: bent knee push-up, functional
strength measurement (eg, lateral step-up, sit-to-stand
test, lifting a box, and stair climbing test), test battery
(eg, jumping a distance of 7 m on 2 ft and 1 ft and
climbing wall bars), and Resistance Training Skills Bat­
tery for Children (eg, push-up, step-up, body-weight
squat, standing overhead press, front support with chest
touches, and suspended row)
• Muscle power: vertical jump, standing long jump, func­
tional strength measurement (eg, overarm throwing,
standing long jump, underarm throwing, and chest
pass), and fitness test (eg, standing broad jump and
20-m sprint). When interpreting the results of these assessments, it
is crucial to consider characteristics of children with DCD,
such as motor planning impairments, which may affect per­
formance outcomes and potentially skew interpretations.9,133
Subsequently, BFS impairments should be viewed as one
facet for addressing greater participation and not as inter­
vention goals. Research Recommendation:
• Examine the psychometric properties specific to the
DCD population of standardized assessments commonly
used in the physical therapy management of children
with DCD.
• Develop or clarify standardized participation and activity
measures that are responsive to change for short inter­
vention durations of 8 to 12 weeks, the typical duration
of physical therapy intervention for children with DCD.
• Identify movement quality characteristics and key activi­
ties to observe in infants and young children that predict
DCD.
• Conduct longitudinal studies of participation to inform
intervention decisions and an understanding of partici­
pation restrictions over the lifespan.
[B] Action Statement 4: USE SHARED DECISION-­
MAKING TO ESTABLISH MEANINGFUL GOALS. For
children at risk for DCD or diagnosed with DCD, PTs should
use shared decision-making with the child and family to
establish measurable, child-centered functional goals based
on their participation priorities during the initial and subse­
quent examinations. (Evidence Quality: II, Recommenda­
tion Strength: Moderate)
Action Statement Profile.

318 Sargent et al
­parents/caregivers, and relevant service providers (eg, IEP team
and outpatient rehabilitation services). Child-centered goals
must be meaningful and relevant to what the child wants,
needs, or is expected to do in their environment. Collabora­
tive goal-setting helps the PT understand the child’s activities,
perceived needs, limitations, and strengths. It guides the PT,
child, and family to focus the plan of care on their participation
priorities.134–137
Shared decision-making is a process in which clinicians and
the child and their family make decisions together using the best
available evidence, balancing risks and expected outcomes with
the child and family’s preferences and values.137 Incorporating
shared decision-making enhances the child’s satisfaction and
adherence to interventions, particularly when goals align with
the cultural and social expectations for participation.8,137,138 This
approach also improves perceived quality of care, motivation,
and tracking of progress among children and families.139–142
Parents/caregivers report the desire to collaborate dur­
ing goal development because they want to leverage the PT’s
knowledge to help ensure goals are appropriate and attaina­
ble.140,141 If children and families voice difficulty establishing
participation priorities, the PT can facilitate goal development
through the use of tools such as the PEGS system, described in
Action Statement 3. Functional goals can be written as whole or part of the
­participation-related task.131 An example of a whole goal
might be playing a game of kickball at recess, whereas goals
for kicking or catching a playground ball, or running to a
base, would be part of a larger participation goal. If progress
toward activity and participation goals is unable to be met,
it is appropriate to assess the BFS that may impede the pro­
gress of the goal. Intervention may be required to address BFS
impairments or incorporate environmental adaptations that
directly support the achievement of participation goals,10,49,87
but impairment-based goals should not be created in isola­
tion. Solely addressing impairments may not directly improve
activity or participation. Goals should be specific and measurable, including who
will complete what task and how, under what conditions, and
in a specific time frame.135 Activity- and participation-based
goals may lack standardized ways to measure baseline, pro­
gress, or attainment. Three options can be used to rate the
child’s performance objectively and are responsive to change
with therapeutic intervention: the COPM,110,111,143,144 Goal
Attainment Scaling (GAS),111,143–145 and the Performance Qual­
ity Rating Scale (PQRS).146 All 3 provide structure to define a
range of outcomes for each goal. The goals can then be objec­
tively measured at baseline and at regular intervals by the PT
(eg, GAS and PQRS) and/or the parent/caregiver (eg, COPM)
to track progress and attainment.

Multiple tools, such as the
COPM and PQRS, can be used together to document progress
by both the PT and parent/caregiver for a more comprehensive
picture of the child’s progress. Education: Although therapists may intend to create col­
laborative child-centered goals, many parents/caregivers feel
they are not adequately involved in the goal-setting process.141
Angeli et al found low agreement between what the parents/
caregivers and therapists believed the goals were that the
child was working toward in therapy.141 Goal agreement may
improve with appropriate caregiver and therapist goal-setting
education.141 Many therapists may not be familiar with all 3
recommended goal-setting options. Therapists must receive
education about the tools and proper interviewing techniques
to ensure they incorporate the child’s and parent/caregiver’s
perspectives into their measurable therapy goals.141
Research Recommendation:
• Determine best practices for using shared decision-­
making to establish measurable, child-centered, func­
tional goals for children at risk for DCD or diagnosed
with DCD based on the participation priorities of the
child and family.
[P] Action Statement 5: ESTABLISH COLLABORATIVE
PLAN OF CARE. PTs should use shared decision-making with
the child, family, and other relevant service providers to estab­
lish a collaborative plan of care that may include referral of chil­
dren to their primary care provider when signs and symptoms
are suggestive of DCD and the child has not been diagnosed or
if there are red flags or concerns for other medical conditions.
(Evidence Quality: V, Recommendation Strength: Best Prac­
tice)
Action Statement Profile. Aggregate Evidence Quality:
Level V, based on CPGs, the APTA Guide to PT Practice, review
articles, and expert clinical consensus. Benefits:
• Referral to the child’s primary care provider may assist in
timely attainment of a DCD diagnosis, differential diag­
nosis, and/or referral to other healthcare or educational
professionals to ensure timely, coordinated interventions.
• Shared decision-making to establish a collaborative plan
of care may result in improved adherence to the plan of
care and better clinical outcomes.
• Collaboration among healthcare providers and relevant

chunks.text:
ents/caregivers, and clinician agree on how interventions will
be delivered, by whom, how often, and what to do if adherence
dwindles. Readers are referred to Moore and Kaplan137 for a
review of shared decision-making techniques.
Referrals: PTs should refer to the child’s primary care
provider if there are red flags or concerns related to medical,
developmental, emotional, or other conditions.102 Examples
of red flags requiring immediate referral include: history of
trauma, headaches or blurred vision, deterioration in motor
skills, or significant hypertonia or hypotonia.102 Referrals
may occur after the initial screening, following the exam­
ination, or anytime throughout the episode of care if con­
cerns arise.
Informing a DCD diagnosis: When parents/caregivers
desire a diagnosis of DCD and if the information gathered from
Action Statements 1 to 3 indicates below age level coordination
concerns or DCD is suspected, the PT should provide a physical
therapy report to the child’s primary care provider, psychologist,
or interprofessional team. This report should include informa­
tion relevant to the DSM-5-TR criteria for DCD. This supports
timely diagnosis, allowing the medical professional or team to
evaluate the 4 DSM-5-TR criteria using their own findings along
with the PT’s documentation. The PT may also provide general
information on DCD, such as diagnostic details (Table 4) or the
physical therapy patient management algorithm for DCD (Fig­
ure 1), and other supplemental tools designed for this guideline.
Research Recommendations:
• Data are needed on the number of children with coor­
dination difficulties, at risk for DCD, or diagnosed with
DCD who are examined by PTs and are referred for con­
cerns about coexisting or exclusionary conditions, or
confirmation of the DCD diagnosis. These data would
establish the incidence of conditions discovered during
the examination process and the effectiveness of referral
patterns.
• Investigate best practices for how PTs can use shared
decision-making with a collaborative team to establish
a comprehensive, multidisciplinary plan of care for
DCD.

APPROACHES TO INTERVENTION. For children at risk
for DCD or diagnosed with DCD, PTs should use and doc­
ument task-oriented approaches to intervention, guided by
the child’s goals and meaningful activities, with BFS interven­
tions used only when directly supporting the achievement of
the child’s goals. (Evidence Quality: I, Recommendation
Strength: Strong)
Action Statement Profile. Aggregate Evidence Quality:
Level I based on high-quality SRs with meta-analyses and RCTs.
Benefits:
• Improved outcomes in children receiving task-oriented
approaches, such as motor skill training and the Cog­
nitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance
(CO-OP) approach, compared with standard care or no
intervention.

should use task-oriented approaches to intervention that target
the child’s goals and are guided by activities that are meaning­
ful to the child. Task-oriented approaches are based on the­
ories of motor control and motor learning and focus on goal
attainment.10,49,134,147,148 The 2 task-oriented approaches with
the strongest evidence are motor skill training10,49,87,147,149 and
CO-OP.134 For further details on the evidence supporting this
recommendation, refer to Supplemental Digital Content 1,
Common principles of task-oriented approaches include:
• Part to whole practice
• Task-specific practice with multiple repetitions
• Task-specific practice in variable environments and con­
texts
• Progressive increases in environmental and task demands
• Facilitated self-discovery using individualized methods
(eg, video viewing of task practice and guidance toward
task components that are modifiable)
• Appropriate feedback, including augmented feedback,
external feedback, and internal feedback150
Motor skill training: Motor skill training focuses on the
practice of specific motor skills.

chunks.text:
Examples of motor skill train­
ing include fundamental motor skills intervention26 and physi­
cal education interventions focusing on specific motor skills.149
Many RCTs support improvement in motor skill outcomes after
motor skill training.26,27,149,151 Refer to Supplemental Digital
A690 for details on the RCTs investigating motor skills training. In addition, many SRs support large effect sizes for motor
skill interventions, compared with standard care or no inter­
vention.10,25,49,147,148 However, most of these SRs included com­
munity physical activities, such as active video gaming (AVG),
aquatics, soccer, and trampoline training as part of the analysis,
and reported moderate to high heterogeneity secondary to the
variety of intervention approaches, clinical settings (school,
community, home), intervention doses, child-chosen goals,
intervention methods (group vs. individual) and diagnostic
variation in the sample groups (at risk for DCD vs. probable
DCD).25,49,134,147,148
Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Perfor­
mance (CO-OP): The CO-OP approach integrates motor con­
trol, motor learning, and cognitive behavioral theories.134 The
benefits of CO-OP for children with DCD include increased goal
attainment, increased confidence, increased ­cognitive-strategy
use, and neuroplastic changes.134 Brain imaging has revealed
measurable changes to cerebellar and cortical gray matter vol­
ume after CO-OP, supporting that CO-OP induces neuroplastic
adaptations in brain regions involved in motor planning, exe­
cution, and cognitive control.56,152
Results are consistent across studies that CO-OP effects
positive changes, but the quality of evidence of CO-OP for
children with DCD is mixed and varies by outcome. There
is moderate quality of evidence for improved performance
of child-chosen goals, low-quality evidence for changes in
participation, and very low quality of evidence for changes in
general motor skills and performance of an untrained activity
as indicators of generalization and transfer.134 These findings
highlight the importance of choosing impactful goals that
target the participation priorities and focusing intervention
on the child’s goals. Training is required to perform CO-OP
with fidelity.134

will support attainment of the child’s goals.153 It is important
to note that impairment-based interventions alone do not
have a significant impact on motor performance49 and are
not recommended in isolation. The GDG recommends that
PTs use task-oriented approaches combined with targeted
impairment-based interventions only when relevant to the
child’s goals. Interventions for Preschool and Kindergarten-Aged
Children With Coordination Difficulties: School-based
interventions are now being developed and tested for children
under 6 years of age with coordination difficulties or at risk
for DCD, with positive results.149,154 Identifying and providing
targeted task-oriented approaches to intervention earlier in
childhood has the potential to positively impact the motor tra­
jectory of children with coordination difficulties and improve
their future motor function. Research Recommendation:
• Determine the efficacy of task-oriented approaches
focusing on specific motor skills to improve motor per­
formance and participation of children with or at risk for
DCD.
• Determine the efficacy of early task-oriented approaches
during preschool or kindergarten on the motor trajec­
tory of children with or at risk for DCD.
• Determine the mechanisms supporting change with
task-oriented approaches to intervention.
• Determine best practice methods for tailoring task-­
oriented approaches to the individual needs or contexts
of children with DCD.
[A] Action Statement 7: RECOMMEND COMMUNITY
PHYSICAL ACTIVITIES. After appraising the appropriate­
ness for the child, PTs should recommend evidence-informed,
community physical activities to complement task-oriented
approaches to intervention for children at risk for or diagnosed
with DCD. (Evidence Quality: I, Recommendation Strength:
Strong)
Action Statement Profile. Aggregate Evidence Quality:
Level I based on CPGs, SRs, and RCTs
Benefits:
• Evidence-informed physical activities may improve
outcomes when combined with task-oriented inter­
ventions.
• Evidence-informed physical activities may reinforce the
child’s goals and may promote child participation in
physical activities with family and peers in the commu­
nity. Risk, Harm, and Cost:
• Most evidence-informed, community physical activities
require a trained specialist and/or occur in an environ­
ment outside of school or clinic settings.
• Specific evidence-informed, community physical activi­
ties may not be available in all geographic regions.
• The costs of evidence-informed, community physical
activities may be a burden for families, due to program
fees, time, travel, and equipment.
• Active video gaming may decrease time spent playing
outdoors.155
• Instructors or coaches in community settings may not
be familiar with DCD and thus may need guidance in
appropriate instructional strategies for children with
DCD. Benefit–Harm Assessment: Preponderance of benefit.

Value Judgments: PTs should recommend the strongest
evidence-informed physical activities to augment task-oriented
approaches that align with the child’s goals and engage the
child. Participation in physical activities within the community
that are enjoyable for the child may improve self-confidence
and quality of life outcomes. Intentional Vagueness: The list of evidence-informed
physical activities is limited to published studies and may not
represent all activities that might reinforce the child’s goals. There is no clear evidence that individual or small group sports
should be recommended over larger team sports for children
with DCD. However, extrapolation of evidence about possible

chunks.text:
322 Sargent et al
Supporting Evidence and Clinical Interpretation.
­Evidence-informed physical activities are intended to com­
plement physical therapy intervention and should not replace
task-oriented approaches to intervention. These activities typ­
ically: (1) take place in the home or community, (2) align with
the goals of the child and their parent/caregiver, and (3) are
not generally part of direct physical therapy intervention. Such
activities may include task-oriented approaches, strategies to
address BFS impairments, initiatives to promote physical fit­
ness, or activities that encourage age-appropriate engagement
with peers or family members. For further details on the evi­
dence supporting this recommendation, refer to Supplemental
lww.com/PPT/A690. Level I and II Evidence From Small Randomized Con­
trolled Trials. Physical Activities: These physical activities
described in small RCTs have demonstrated the potential to
improve motor performance of children with DCD:
• Equine therapy to improve gait parameters,158
• Futsal taught using a specific approach to improve motor
proficiency,159
• Table tennis to improve aiming and catching skills,160
• Tai chi or muscle power training to reduce falls,161
• Trampoline training to improve motor performance,162
• Taekwondo (TKD)’s effectiveness is inconsistent. One
RCT found no significant difference between TKD and
jogging for improving motor skills and balance,163 while
another demonstrated improved single-leg balance con­
trol compared with no intervention.121,164
Active video gaming (AVG)165: AVG refers to interactive
gaming that involves physical activity, as opposed to passive,
handheld gaming devices. Two SRs examined AVG’s effective­
ness.166,167 One review found that most children enjoyed and
adhered to AVG interventions.167 Both reviews found low-­
quality evidence supporting benefits for activity and BFS out­
comes, including strength, anaerobic performance, and aerobic
fitness.166,167 The reviews noted that studies often found similar
results to control or comparison groups. The only RCT pub­
lished since these SRs found similar results between AVG and
task-oriented training.168 Due to a small sample size, the study
may not have had sufficient power to detect a statistically sig­
nificant difference between the intervention groups. An impor­
tant finding from one study was that children in the AVG group
spent less time outside on the weekends.155 Therefore, PTs must
educate children and their parents/caregivers not to displace
AVG with other productive physical activities.

chunks.text:
Enhancing physical activity participation: The Clinical
Practice Guideline to Enhance Physical Activity Participation
for Children With DCD in Canada includes 50 recommenda­
tions to promote and enhance the participation and integration
of children with DCD into physical activities that occur in the
home, school, community, or rehabilitation clinic.169 While this
guideline does not review specific activities, it provides strate­
gies and considerations for parents, instructors, and clinicians
when selecting activities, modulating difficulty, and providing
feedback and supervision to enhance success. Research Recommendation:
• Clarify the efficacy of evidence-informed community
physical activities to improve motor performance or
increase participation in physical activities or recreation
for children at risk for or with a diagnosis of DCD.
[A] Action Statement 8: USE SMALL GROUP OR INDIVID­
UAL SESSIONS. For children at risk for DCD or diagnosed
with DCD, PTs should document and deliver interventions
using individual (1:1) or small group (1:4–6) sessions. (Evi­
dence Quality: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong)
Action Statement Profile. Aggregate Evidence Quality:
Level I based on SRs and results from intervention studies
using small and large groups. Benefits:
• Improved outcomes have been demonstrated in children
receiving individual and small group interventions.
• Physical therapy delivered in small groups (1:4–6) to
address both social and motor objectives may be deliv­
ered at a lower cost and be most applicable in camp or
community settings. Risk, Harm, and Cost:
• Child anxiety may increase if groups are too large.
• Social group dynamics are unpredictable and may impact
individual outcomes.
• Time constraints for small group sessions may be limit­
ing for parents and children.
• Space and resource availability may be limited.
• Group-based charges may not be covered by third party
payers. Benefit–Harm Assessment: Preponderance of benefit. Value Judgements: Caution should be taken when using
group-based interventions by monitoring each child for signs
of increased anxiety, avoidance of group participation, or lack
of enjoyment. Children should be given the opportunity to
express how they feel about an intervention method. Intentional Vagueness: None. Role of Child/Parent Preferences: Parents/caregivers and
other relevant service providers provide valuable information
on the effects that an intervention may have on their child. Children may have preferences for either individual or small
group sessions that should be considered when developing
interventions. Exclusions: None. Differences of Opinion: None. Quality Improvement: Documentation of outcomes and
the sessions using group versus individual approaches can con­
tribute to patient registries.
