chunks.text:
Implementation and Audit:
• Documentation forms may need to be revised to include
group and individual options.
• Audit the types of interventions using group and individ­
ual sessions and the outcome measures used. Supporting Evidence and Clinical Interpretation. There
is evidence to support both small group (1:4–6) and individual
intervention sessions as beneficial for children with coordina­
tion difficulties, at risk for DCD, or who have a diagnosis of
DCD.10,148,170 The evidence is inconclusive on whether an indi­
vidual approach is superior for improving motor performance,
components of physical fitness, or quality of life outcomes
compared with a group-based approach.148,170 Large effect sizes
on motor performance were found for both group (Cohen d =
1.46) and individual (Cohen d = 1.05) sessions.148 A combina­
tion of group and individual sessions also yielded significant
improvements in performance and satisfaction with ADLs.170
The exact ratio for group-based intervention needs fur­
ther investigation. Recommendations on the ideal group
size cannot be determined based on the data, but we know
that groups of between 4 and 6 children have been used, are
manageable, and effective with one therapist and an optional
assistant.148 PTs should be aware of adverse events reported
for children participating in a large group with a 5:11 ratio
compared with 3 smaller groups with ratios of 2 to 3:4 to 5.156
Children in the large group with the 5:11 ratio showed higher
anxiety and lower levels of enjoyment, even though parents
noted a decrease in peer problems and an improvement in
rate of function as measured using the Children Activity
Scale.156 The GDG recommends that PTs be mindful of each
child’s response during group sessions. A combination of
small group and individual sessions could be used to encour­
age participation with peers, generalize skills within natural
circumstances, and address individual goals. The child’s com­
fort with and benefit from group interventions must be con­
sidered a priority over any potential cost savings by providing
physical therapy in groups. Research Recommendation:
• Clarify the factors that influence decisions about group
versus individual sessions, such as participants’ sociocul­
tural factors, motor impairment severity, or diagnostic
status of at risk for DCD versus diagnosed with DCD.
• Determine optimal combinations of group and/or indi­
vidual sessions for improving motor performance of chil­
dren with DCD.
[B] Action Statement 9: PROVIDE APPROPRIATE INTER­
VENTION DOSAGE. For children at risk for DCD or diagnosed
with DCD, PTs should design episodic intervention plans with
high practice frequencies, using a combination of direct services
and home, school, and community opportunities. (Evidence
Quality: II, Recommendation Strength: Moderate)
Action Statement Profile. Aggregate Evidence Quality:
Level II based on an SR with a meta-analysis.

Benefits:
• Improved physical therapy outcomes with appropriate
intervention frequency and duration.
• Combining direct physical therapy services with home
practice and community/recreation activities promotes
appropriate social participation for children and families. Risk, Harm, and Cost:
• Increased energy, cost, and time associated with increas­
ing intervention dosage.
• Increased demands on space and resources in different
settings.
• Increasing dosage may cause increased anxiety and
decreased enjoyment for the child. Benefit–harm Assessment: Preponderance of benefits. Value Judgements: A higher practice frequency is neces­
sary to achieve short-term outcomes. However, the practice
schedule design may be dependent on the PT’s experience to
creatively encourage practice with non-PT’s (eg, parents/car­
egivers, teachers, physical education teachers, paraprofession­
als, coaches, and community activity providers). More home/
community-based opportunities for practice may be optimal
depending on financial resources. PTs need to closely collabo­
rate with the child/family to adapt the plan of care based on the
child’s responses and the parent/caregiver resources. Intentional Vagueness: None. Role of Patient/Parent Preferences:
• Child and parent/caregiver adherence to the home pro­
gram directed by the PT is needed to obtain the optimal
dosage for benefits.
• Parents/caregivers and the child need to accurately report
their ability to implement a recommended intervention
plan based on their resources and the child’s capacity. Exclusions: None. Differences of Opinion: None. Quality Assurance:
• Dosage recommendations for clinicians and consum­
ers provide guidance for evidence-based interventions
including the time commitment needed to see meaning­
ful improvement.
• Objective data on intervention dosages (physical ther­
apy, home programs, and evidence-informed physical
activities) contribute to patient registries. Implementation and Audit:
• Documentation forms and electronic records may need
to be revised to include intervention approaches (phys­
ical therapy, home or school practice, and evidence-­
informed physical activities) and dosage parameters. PTs

chunks.text:
324 Sargent et al
should document practice frequencies from direct ser­
vice, home, or school practice, and evidence-informed
physical activities to the extent practical.
• Audit intervention approaches and respective dosages to
determine the overall benefits to children. Supporting Evidence and Clinical Interpretation. The
literature on therapeutic dosage is quite variable. Yu et al49 con­
ducted an SR of 66 studies on motor skills training for chil­
dren with DCD, which yielded 18 studies for a meta-analysis. Therapeutic dosages were reported as the length of sessions,
total number of sessions/week, total number of weeks, and
total minutes of sessions; practice schedules were not provided
solely as direct intervention by a PT, but included a variety of
delivery methods and service providers.49 Interventions varied:
44% were task-oriented, 15% process-oriented (focused on
BFS), 18% combined task-oriented and process-oriented, and
23% were undefined.49
Yu et al49 found the session totals were highly variable,
ranging from 10 minutes to 6 hours, 1 to 5 times per week
for 4 to 24 weeks (180–2500 minutes). The most significant
factors that impacted immediate motor performance in the
meta-­analysis were the total minutes of intervention (approx­
imately 100/wk) and the frequency of sessions per week.49
Practice schedules of 4 to 5 times per week (Hedges g = 1.67,
P < .001; large effect),49 over at least 9 weeks (Hedges g =
0.93, P < .001; large effect),49 regardless of the length of the
sessions or total number of sessions, resulted in significant
improvement in motor performance. However, even 2 to 3
times per week (Hedges g = 0.80, P = .008; large effect)49
and once a week (Hedges g = 0.38, P = .003; small effect)
resulted in improved short-term motor performance gains
with increased practice over time. The GDG is not recommending a single definitive pre­
scribed dosage for intervention at this time. The evidence sup­
ports frequent practice scheduled over several weeks, or until
the goal-related outcomes are achieved. The PT should deter­
mine the number of direct intervention sessions needed to
achieve a cumulative practice schedule of 100 minutes per week
for an average of 9 weeks to achieve a goal-related task, depend­
ing on the goal complexity and the child’s motor limitations. The practice schedule may include a combination of direct
intervention sessions, home program practice, or practice with
school personnel, and community physical activities related to
the intervention outcomes. An optimal example of this type of
schedule is: 1 to 2 direct physical therapy sessions/week, with
a home program and/or additional time to practice during the
school day for school-based settings. Community physical
activities should be recommended to complement the primary
physical therapy intervention. Measurable progress toward the
child’s goals would determine the duration of intervention.

sample schedule may be implemented in a variety of settings

MAKING TO ESTABLISH A HOME PROGRAM. For chil­
dren at risk for DCD or diagnosed with DCD, PTs should use
shared decision-making with the child, parents/caregivers, and
other relevant service providers to establish a meaningful home
program that may include education, coaching, motor skill
practice, or community physical activities to support attain­

family and peers. (Evidence Quality: II, Recommendation
Strength: Moderate)

• Shared decision-making enhances the relevance of edu­

chunks.text:
One home management option is instruction on effective
teaching methods and motor learning techniques to implement
at home, school, or in the community.8 Small qualitative ­studies
investigating parents’ experiences of a CO-OP home program
found that parents enjoyed seeing their children experience
successes and the difference these made in their children’s
lives.171 However, parents reported 3 challenges: (1) finding
the time to do the home programs, (2) shifting children’s atti­
tudes and existing parent–child relationships because CO-OP
requires that children are guided to perform tasks versus having
tasks done for them, and (3) difficulty implementing CO-OP at
home, which parent/caregivers felt could have been improved
by more practice under therapist supervision.171
Education about practice, repetition for motor learning,
and attaining new skills supports physical therapy interven­
tions and the general health of the child. Parents/caregivers
and other relevant service providers may need training and
directed practice in task-oriented methods and principles of
motor learning to encourage a child’s success.8 A thorough
list of specific adult education methods used for parents of
children with DCD does not exist in the literature. Parents/
caregivers should be directed to the CanChild M.A.T.C.H.
framework, which suggests that they: (1) Modify the envi­
ronment, (2) Alter expectations, (3) Teach strategies, (4)
Change the environment, and (5) Help by understanding.172
tion-disorder
Examples of teaching strategies the PT should encourage
with parents/caregivers and other relevant service providers
gathered from DCD studies and other task-oriented, motor
learning literature include:
• breaking the task into smaller, simple components;
• beginning with decreased environmental and task
demands;
• repetition of task components followed by whole task
practice;
• gradually increasing task demands until the child can
generalize skills to perform the task;
• gradually modifying feedback strategies to support inde­
pendent task performance; and
• encouraging self-discovery of problem areas and motor
imagery if appropriate.81
Another home management option is promoting and
enhancing participation in physical activities with family
and peers. A good resource for strategies to enhance phys­
ical activity for children with DCD is the Clinical Practice
Guideline to Enhance Physical Activity Participation for
Children With DCD in Canada.169 This CPG includes 50
recommendations to promote and enhance the participa­
tion and integration of children with DCD into physical
activities that occur in the home, school, community, or
rehabilitation clinic.169

Research Recommendation:
• Investigate how PTs can collaborate with and coach par­
ents/caregivers and other relevant service providers to
facilitate long-term training effects and general health of
children with or at risk for DCD. III. Monitoring Children at Risk for DCD or Diagnosed
With DCD
[P] Action Statement 11: MEASURE PROGRESS TOWARDS
GOALS. For children at risk for DCD or diagnosed with DCD,
PTs should regularly measure progress toward their goals to deter­
mine with parents/caregivers whether physical therapy interven­
tions should be modified, new goals should be established, or if
the children should be transitioned from direct intervention to
annual or semi-annual physical therapy reevaluations. (Evidence
Quality: V; Recommendation Strength: Best Practice)
Action Statement Profile. Aggregate Evidence Quality:
Review articles and expert clinical consensus. Benefits:
• Transitioning from direct intervention when activity/par­
ticipation goals are met is a cost-efficient method of care.
• An annual or semi-annual physical therapy reevaluation
may be beneficial to review goals, consider goal-oriented
reinitiation of direct physical therapy, review home man­
agement suggestions and activity modifications and pro­
gressions, review evidence-informed community physical
activity options, make appropriate referrals as concerns
change with increasing age, and provide the child’s pri­
mary care provider and other relevant service providers
with a summary of the child’s current motor performance. Risk, Harm, and Cost: Reevaluations and possible subse­
quent interventions may add to the cost of care. Benefit–Harm Assessment: Preponderance of benefit. Value Judgements: An annual or semi-annual physical
therapy reevaluation is in the best interest of the child, reflects
­family-centered care, and acknowledges that DCD is a develop­
mental condition that may require episodic intervention over
many years. Intentional Vagueness: The GDG is vague about the
timing for reevaluation of children with DCD. Timelines for
­follow-up are not discussed in the literature and are at the
discretion of the PT in consultation with the parent/caregiver,
child’s primary care provider, and other professionals. Families
should be encouraged to request physical therapy reevaluations
following growth spurts or when new movement challenges are
not responding to family-initiated modifications.

• Parents/caregivers may choose not to reinitiate direct
physical therapy if it places undue burden on the family
for travel, time, or finances.
• Parents should be advised that once their child is tran­
sitioned to annual or semi-annual evaluations, they may
request physical therapy reevaluations if they have new
concerns or goals for their child, and resources are avail­
able for services.
• The impact of DCD on quality of life across the lifespan68,77,80
should be discussed with parents/caregivers over the epi­
sode of care and at discharge, along with guidance about
how PTs can assist with adaptations as needs arise.
• The impact of DCD on quality of life should be queried
with adolescents with DCD to address concerns about
receiving episodic interventions and challenges that arise
with age and social demands.78
Exclusions: None. Differences of Opinion: None. Quality Improvement: Long-term data about frequency
and dosage of physical therapy episodes of care may allow
therapists to share information with parents about the expected
amount and types of lifetime interventions for a child with
DCD. Implementation and Audit:
• Educate parents/caregivers about the potential need for
periodic episodes of physical therapy care based on child
or parent/caregiver goals. Reasons to reinitiate direct
physical therapy would be functional decline or new
functional goals important for the child’s participation in
the home, school, or community.
• Access resources on the Rehabilitation Measures Data­
base for updated psychometric properties of standard­
ized assessments, including minimal clinically important
ures.

itiated and the overall frequency and dosage of physical
therapy or referral to other services per year, per child. Supporting Evidence and Clinical Interpretation. PTs

chunks.text:
transitioned from direct intervention to annual or semi-annual
physical therapy reevaluations.
Since most children with DCD do not outgrow their motor
limitations,8,102 regular physical therapy reevaluations are
necessary throughout childhood to review concerns, goals,
consider goal-oriented reinitiation of direct physical therapy,
review home management suggestions and activity modifica­
tions and progressions, review community physical activity
options, make appropriate referrals, and provide the child’s
primary care provider and other relevant service providers with
a summary of the child’s current motor performance. Parents/
caregivers should be educated that their child with or at risk for
DCD may require multiple physical therapy episodes of care
throughout childhood, and also should be educated on when a
physical therapy reassessment is indicated.
Research Recommendations:
• Develop long-term follow-up data to study children with
DCD to describe factors and adaptations contributing to
successful adult life.
• Determine the extent to which adolescents and adults
with DCD benefit from physical therapy interventions
to address specific goals related to school, recreation, or
employment.

Summary
A review of the literature through January 2025 reaffirms and
updates the 2020 DCD CPG. The 2026 DCD CPG includes
11 graded action statements that address physical therapy
contributions to the diagnostic process, examination and eval­
uation including recommended outcome measures, shared
­decision-making to establish meaningful goals and home pro­
grams, collaborative plans of care including referral to other
providers and dosage considerations, evidence-based interven­
tion including task-oriented approaches to intervention and
community physical activities, progress monitoring, transition
to annual or semi-annual reassessments, implementation and
compliance recommendations, and research recommendations.
Strategies for guideline implementation, additional methodo­
logical processes, evidence tables, and a summary of research
recommendations are available in Supplemental Digital Con­
sheets for examination and intervention for DCD and summa­
ries for families and professionals are available as supplemental
clinical-practice-guidelines/).
